Born Treorchy, Wales. Wikidata structured record. Wikipedia corroborates.
Died Esher, Surrey, England. Wikidata and Wikipedia agree.
Davies conceived packet-switching in 1965 after attending IFIP Congress in New York and visiting MIT. Term 'packet' coined same year after consulting a linguist for translatability.
Term 'packet' selected 1965 after consulting a linguist, chosen for cross-language translatability. NPL proposal published 1966.
NPL proposal 'Proposal for the Development of a National Communications Service for On-line Data Processing' published 1966.
NPL Mark I network achieved full operational status January 1970. First operational packet-switched network. Construction directed 1968-69 with elements going live early 1969.
Born St. Louis, Missouri. Wikipedia.
Died Arlington, Massachusetts. Wikipedia.
'Intergalactic Computer Network' concept formulated August 1962 at BBN. Memo to colleagues April 23, 1963. This is the specimen's surprise_priority conjecture.
IPTO founded, Licklider as first director from October 1962. He served until July 1964 (first term).
Born New Haven, Connecticut. Wikipedia.
Internet Society officially established December 11 1992 by Vint Cerf, Bob Kahn, and Lyman Chapin. Wikipedia states this date explicitly.
Born New York City. Wikipedia.
Born April 20, 1931. Wikipedia. Still living as of source.
Planning for CYCLADES began 1971. Design and staffing started 1972. First demonstration November 1973 with three hosts and one packet switch.
Louis Pouzin coined the term 'datagram' by combining 'data' and 'telegram' during CYCLADES development. Also introduced 'catenet' concept 1973 for interconnected packet-switched networks.

CYCLADES forced to shut down by 1981. Funding cut in late 1970s (sources say c.1978 but no exact date found). French PTT (DGT) chose Transpac/X.25 over connectionless datagram approach. Network offline 1981.

value: French PTT (DGT) cut CYCLADES funding c.1978; network offline 1981. PTT invoked state monopoly on data transmission to block government funding of a competitor to Transpac.

Minitel pilot trial July 15 1980 in Saint-Malo (55 customers). Expanded to 2500 autumn 1980, 4000 in May 1981. Full commercial service launched 1982 with 120,000 terminals by end of 1983.

value: dissolved
notes: France Télécom discontinued Minitel on June 30, 2012. Attributed to operational costs and declining customer interest. ~800,000 terminals still in operation at shutdown. Displaced by the Internet/Web.
X.25 finalized in 'The Orange Book' 1976 at CCITT plenary assembly. Standard approved at September 1976 CCITT plenary.

value: faded
notes: JANET closed its X.25 service in August 1997. North American X.25 networks started declining early 1990s as Frame Relay/IP replaced them. BT X.25 service persisted to 2019 (niche). Status: faded (niche persists in aviation/amateur radio but not mainstream).
OSI Reference Model formally published 1984 as ISO/IEC 7498 and ITU-T X.200, following May 1983 merger of CCITT and ISO documents. ISO work began 1977.

value: faded
notes: GOSIP requirement dropped 1995 (FIPS 146-2 allowing TCP/IP). From 1995 interest in OSI implementations declined sharply. The OSI model itself survives as a teaching framework but OSI protocols never achieved scale. Status: faded (model persists academically; protocols dead).

value: GOSIP v1 published August 1988; FIPS 146-1 adopted February 15 1989; enforcement began August 15 1990 requiring OSI compliance for federal procurement. US National Research Council 1985 recommended migrating FROM TCP/IP TO OSI.

source.title: Government Open Systems Interconnection Profile — Wikipedia

notes: D6 friction: government procurement mandate. GOSIP v1 August 1988 per UK CCTA and US sources. FIPS 146-1 date and enforcement date from GOSIP search results cross-referencing RFC 1169. UK: 4th/final UK GOSIP 1991. US GOSIP dropped 1995 via FIPS 146-2.

value: GOSIP 1988-1990 mandate suppressed TCP/IP federal procurement for ~5 years despite TCP/IP being operational since 1983. The mandate was largely toothless: lack of OSI products encouraged TCP/IP purchase anyway.

source.title: Government Open Systems Interconnection Profile — Wikipedia

notes: D6 friction: adoption lag created by procurement mandate. RFC 1169 (August 1990) explicitly discusses GOSIP's role. The mandate created a 5-year headwind for TCP/IP in government.

source.title: Delivery of the First IMP to UCLA — History of Computer Communications

notes: First IMP delivered to UCLA August 30, 1969 (air-shipped to beat Labor Day deadline). BBN Wikipedia says 'September' but multiple sources including ICANN blog confirm August 30 delivery. First message sent October 29 1969 (UCLA to SRI, 'lo' before crash). Four-node network December 5 1969.

Cerf and Kahn published 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication' IEEE Trans. Comms May 1974. RFC 675 (Cerf, Dalal, Sunshine) published December 1974 — approximately 7 months from paper to RFC. Note: Kahn not listed as RFC 675 author; Dalal and Sunshine added.
RFC 675 (December 1974) contains the first attested use of 'internet' as shorthand for internetwork. Authors: Cerf, Dalal, Sunshine.

value: 7 months: Cerf-Kahn paper May 1974 -> RFC 675 December 1974
notes: D6 friction: publication lag. From the internetworking paper (May 1974) to the first formal Internet specification RFC (December 1974) was approximately 7 months.

Jonathan Postel proposed splitting TCP into TCP + IP in TCP/IP version 4 (1978), creating the layered architecture with IP as connectionless datagram layer. This created the 'narrow waist' hourglass architecture.

ARPANET NCP->TCP/IP flag day: January 1 1983. DoD declared TCP/IP official standard March 1982 with transition deadline Jan 1 1983. Hosts not converted lost ARPANET access. Transition complete by June 1983.

value: ~9 years from Cerf-Kahn paper (May 1974) to operational flag day (January 1 1983); ~4 years from RFC 675 (December 1974) to TCP/IP v4 split (1978); ~5 years from split to flag day
notes: D6 friction: propagation/adoption lag. Total lag from specification to operational adoption was ~9 years. This is the specimen's key D6 bandwidth/propagation datum: a slow distributed cascade vs Manhattan's 33-month fast pull.
NSFNET established 1986 with 6 backbone sites at 56 kbit/s. Upgraded to 1.5 Mbit/s (T-1) July 1988 at 13 nodes; 45 Mbit/s (T-3) November 1991 at 16 nodes.
NSF lifted Acceptable Use Policy ban on commercial traffic in 1991. Commercial ISP business grew rapidly thereafter. First commercial email gateways permitted experimentally 1989.
NSFNET backbone retired April 30 1995. New model: regional backbones + commercial providers (internetMCI, PSINet, SprintLink, ANSNet) exchanging at 4 Network Access Points.

JANET IP Service (JIPS) pilot launched March 1991; by November 1991 IP traffic exceeded X.25 volumes on JANET — one clean tipping-point date for the protocol wars. JANET closed X.25 service August 1997.
US NIST proposed 1994 GOSIP should incorporate TCP/IP and drop OSI requirement; adopted into FIPS 1995. This effectively ended OSI's regulatory backing in the US.
Born October 15, 1944. Wikipedia.
RFC 1 'Host Software' by Steve Crocker published April 7, 1969. First document in the RFC series, originating the open standardization method.
Born April 7, 1944. Wikipedia.
David Clark articulated 'We reject kings, presidents, and voting. We believe in rough consensus and running code.' in 1992 at an IETF meeting. This formalized the IETF's process ethos.

End-to-End Arguments in System Design (Saltzer, Reed, Clark) presented at Second International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems, Paris, April 8-10 1981. Journal version published in ACM Transactions on Computer Systems, vol. 2 no. 4, 1984.
BBN founded October 15, 1948 by Leo Beranek and Richard Bolt. Robert Newman joined 1950 giving the company its final name. Wikipedia.
Cisco founded December 10, 1984 in San Francisco by Leonard Bosack and Sandy Lerner (Stanford). First commercial router (AGS) shipped 1986. IPO February 16 1990 on NASDAQ.

Cisco Advanced Gateway Server (AGS) shipped 1986 as the first commercial multi-protocol router. This operationalized the gateway/router concept at scale, enabling the protocol-wars-era internet buildout.
Born June 8, 1955, London. Wikipedia.

Berners-Lee submitted his web proposal to CERN on March 12, 1989. First successful HTTP client-server communication November 1989. First website published December 20, 1990. Public announcement August 6, 1991.

CERN made web protocol and code royalty-free on April 30 1993, enabling widespread adoption. NCSA Mosaic browser released 1993; thousands of websites emerged. Netscape IPO 1995 triggered dot-com boom.
CERN (European Organization for Nuclear Research) founded 1954. Berners-Lee joined June 1980 as contractor, returned as fellow 1984. W3C founded 1994 at MIT by Berners-Lee.

IETF formally established January 1986, evolving from the Gateway Algorithms and Data Structures (GADS) Task Force. First IETF chair was Mike Corrigan. The IAB predates IETF, deciding in 1986 to divide GADS into two entities.
IETF transitioned from US federal government support to operate under ISOC auspices in 1993, formalized in RFC 1602. Restructured as IETF Administration LLC under ISOC in August 2018.
IETF moved under ISOC auspices 1993, formalized RFC 1602. First executive director appointed 1994; permanent headquarters Reston, Virginia. IETF restructured as LLC under ISOC August 2018.
ISOC officially established December 11 1992. Founders: Vint Cerf, Bob Kahn, Lyman Chapin. Represents the 'handing to the world' step (cascade step 11) in the specimen.

ICANN officially incorporated in California September 30, 1998 with Esther Dyson as founding chairwoman. Jon Postel also listed as founder. Manages DNS, IP addresses, protocol parameters. ICANN is referenced in the specimen (act-isoc: ISOC + ICANN) but has no dedicated subject_id; proposed:<slug> for its own facts.
October 1 2016: ICANN freed from US government oversight; NTIA contract ended. Transition of Internet governance functions to global multistakeholder community. Key governance harvest milestone.

value: September 2024: UN Global Digital Compact adopted by 193 member states as part of the 'Pact for the Future', reaffirming multistakeholder internet governance; WSIS+20 review process launched.
notes: 2024-2026 now-refresh. GDC adopted September 2024 by UN Summit of the Future. WSIS+20 review began May 2024 in Geneva, ends UNGA September 2025. UN Permanent Mechanism for Responsible State Behaviour in Cyberspace operational from March 2026.

value: January 2 2025: US Sixth Circuit Court vacated FCC 2024 net neutrality rules, ruling FCC lacked authority to reclassify ISPs under Title II (post-Loper Bright Chevron-deference reversal).

Baltic Sea BCS East West Interlink and C Lion1 damaged late 2024. ~200 cable outages/year globally per ICPC; 150-200 in 2025 alone. Demonstrates physical vulnerability of child infrastructure.

At ~50% IPv6 penetration in 2026, the child is undergoing a slow protocol transition while maintaining backward compatibility with IPv4. Demonstrates method-continuity of child.

notes: 2024-2026 now-refresh. Governance leadership change at ICANN. Kurt Erik Lindqvist appointment confirmed by Wikipedia.

Born June 13, 1934, New York City. Wikipedia.

Kleinrock thesis proposal 1961 'Information Flow in Large Communication Nets'; doctoral thesis 1962 'Message Delay in Communication Nets with Storage'; published as book 'Communication Nets' 1964. This is queueing theory work, NOT packet-switching invention per the specimen's priority dispute.

value: First ARPANET message sent October 29 1969 at 10:30 p.m. from UCLA to SRI: attempted 'login', only 'lo' transmitted before crash. First four-node ARPANET operational December 5, 1969.

value: DARPA RFP for ARPANET: BBN awarded IMP contract January 1969; first IMP delivered August 30 1969 — approximately 3 years from Taylor's 1966 funding to first deployed node.
notes: D6 friction: propagation from concept to first node: Taylor secured $1M funding February 1966; Larry Roberts as program manager January 1967; BBN contract January 1969; first IMP August 30 1969. ~3.5 year lag from funding decision to first packet.
ARPA created by Eisenhower February 1958 in response to Sputnik (October 4 1957). Became DARPA (Defense) in 1972. Wikipedia Sputnik crisis and SpaceNews confirm February 1958.

value: Sputnik launched October 4 1957; ARPA created February 1958 — 4-month lag from crisis trigger to institutional response; ARPANET first deployed 1969 — 11-year cascade from Sputnik to operational packet network.
notes: D6 friction: propagation/bandwidth fact. The cold-war forcing event (Sputnik) took 11 years to propagate to first operational deployment. This is the macro-cascade lag that distinguishes the Internet from Manhattan's 33-month fast pull.

IPv6 standardized via RFC 2460 December 1998. Superseded by RFC 8200 July 2017 (elevated to Internet Standard). Represents within-child evolution: method-continuous upgrade, not a re-weld. IPv6 adoption ~50% as of June 2026 per Google stats.

INWG co-founded by Steve Crocker 1972. Cerf served as chair. The group attempted international internet standardization 1972-1976 before the CCITT chose X.25 instead. Specimen notes the 1976 INWG compromise was adopted by neither CCITT nor ARPANET.

INWG effectively ended after the 1976 CCITT X.25 approval rejected the INWG compromise. Cerf resigned as chair. The partially-failed sub-weld (sw-inwg). Certainty lower as 'dissolved' date is approximate — Wikipedia article may give different framing.

UUNET began commercial TCP/IP services January 1990; The World STD first commercial ISP late 1989/early 1990. Netscape Navigator with HTTPS December 1994. Netscape IPO 1995. Amazon and eBay 1995. The commercial harvest effectively 'unlocked' 1994-1995 when HTTPS + Netscape + NSF retirement coincided.

Donald Davies worked at NPL 1947-1984 per Wikidata. The NPL network (first operational packet network) ran under his leadership. His departure in 1984 effectively marks the end of the NPL's leadership role in packet-switching research.

value: X.25 public data networks achieved 'large global coverage during the 1980s and into the 1990s'. Examples: TRANSPAC (France), DATAPAC (Canada), Telenet and Tymnet (USA). BT X.25 service persisted to 2019.
notes: D6 friction: propagation fact for rival lineage. X.25 achieved real global deployment before TCP/IP dominance. This is the basis for the specimen's rival-lifecycle-coupling: X.25's peak coverage was real, not notional.

value: DoD declared TCP/IP its official standard March 1982; set January 1 1983 as mandatory cutover deadline. From RFC 675 (December 1974) to DoD mandate (March 1982): ~7.5 year lag to institutional mandate.
notes: D6 friction: adoption lag. From the first internet specification (RFC 675, December 1974) to the DoD institutional mandate (March 1982) was ~7.5 years. This institutional adoption lag is a key D6 bandwidth fact for the specimen.

JANET (Joint Academic Network, UK) went live April 1 1984 with ~50 sites. Not in specimen actors. New proposed node. Key exemplar of X.25 adoption then IP transition (JIPS pilot March 1991; IP exceeded X.25 November 1991; X.25 closed August 1997). Records rival-infrastructure founding date for D6 bandwidth context.
